clinicalPearls: Glycogen storage disease type 0 is an autosomal recessive defect of glycogen synthase, and unlike other GSDs it is a disorder of impaired glycogen synthesis rather than storage
The hepatic form (GYS2) presents in infancy or early childhood with fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia, often in the morning before breakfast
Paradoxically, feeding produces postprandial hyperglycaemia and lactic acidosis because glucose cannot be stored as glycogen
The liver is characteristically not enlarged, distinguishing it from the hepatomegalic glycogenoses
A separate muscle form (GYS1) causes exercise intolerance, cardiomyopathy, and risk of sudden death rather than hypoglycaemia
Management of the hepatic form centres on avoiding prolonged fasting, providing frequent protein-rich meals, and using uncooked cornstarch to maintain overnight glucose
Prognosis is generally good with dietary control, and cognitive outcome improves when hypoglycaemia is prevented
reference.pathophysiology: Glycogen synthase catalyses the addition of glucose units to the growing glycogen chain. In GSD type 0, biallelic variants in GYS2 (liver isoform) or GYS1 (muscle isoform) reduce or abolish enzyme activity, so glycogen synthesis is deficient rather than glycogen being over-accumulated. In the hepatic form the liver cannot lay down glycogen stores during feeding, so during fasting there is no glycogen to mobilise, producing hypoglycaemia with ketosis; ingested glucose is diverted toward lactate, causing postprandial hyperglycaemia and hyperlactataemia. In the muscle form, deficient glycogen limits substrate for exercising muscle and impairs cardiac and skeletal muscle energetics.
additionalDifferentials: Other hepatic glycogen storage diseases (GSD I, III, VI, IX)
Fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis defects
Growth hormone or cortisol deficiency causing fasting hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Paired fasting and postprandial glucose, lactate, and ketone measurements to demonstrate fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia with postprandial hyperlactataemia
Molecular genetic testing of GYS2 (hepatic) or GYS1 (muscle)
Liver ultrasound, typically showing a non-enlarged liver
Metabolic screen including acylcarnitine profile to exclude fatty acid oxidation defects
In the muscle form, echocardiography and assessment of exercise tolerance
redFlags: Recurrent symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or impaired consciousness
Developmental delay suggesting repeated unrecognised hypoglycaemic episodes
Exertional syncope, chest symptoms, or cardiomyopathy in the muscle form
Severe lactic acidosis after carbohydrate loading
reference.prognosis: The hepatic form has a good prognosis when fasting is avoided and overnight glucose is maintained, with normal growth and neurodevelopment; the muscle form carries a risk of cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death and warrants cardiac surveillance.
pitfalls: Overlooking GSD 0 because the liver is not enlarged, unlike most hepatic glycogenoses
Misattributing morning symptoms to idiopathic ketotic hypoglycaemia without paired biochemistry
Failing to recognise postprandial hyperglycaemia and lactic acidosis as a diagnostic clue
Not distinguishing the hepatic and muscle forms, which differ in presentation and risks
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: In the hepatic form, prevent fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia by avoiding prolonged fasting, giving frequent protein-rich meals and uncooked cornstarch to maintain overnight glucose
Limit large high-glycaemic carbohydrate loads that provoke postprandial hyperglycaemia and lactic acidosis
Monitor blood glucose, lactate, ketones and growth, adjusting feed timing and composition accordingly
In the muscle form due to GYS1 variants, undertake cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and advise against strenuous exertion given the risk of cardiomyopathy and sudden death
Coordinate care through a specialist metabolic team and dietitian
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance of GYS2 or GYS1 variants with family testing
